<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:ceros1}
Let $f$ be analytic and locally univalent in a simply connected domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}$, with $Sf=2p$. Then $f$ is univalent in $\Omega$ if and only if no nontrivial solution of \eqref{eq:lineal1} vanishes at two distinct points of $\Omega$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Every solution has the form $u=u_0(c_0+c_1f)$, and $u_0$ does not vanish. The solutions that vanish at $a$ are the multiples of $u_0\,(f-f(a))$, and one of them vanishes also at $b$ exactly when $f(b)=f(a)$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:nehari}
If $f$ is analytic and locally univalent in $\mathbb{D}$ and $\|Sf\|\le2$, then $f$ is univalent in $\mathbb{D}$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that $f(a)=f(b)$ with $a\ne b$. Let $\sigma$ be an automorphism of the disk that carries the real diameter onto the hyperbolic geodesic through $a$ and $b$. By the invariance of the norm, $g=f\circ\sigma$ satisfies $\|Sg\|\le2$ and takes the same value at two points of the interval $(-1,1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ceros1} there is a nontrivial solution $u$ of $u''+pu=0$, with $2p=Sg$, that vanishes at those two points; since its zeros are isolated, we may take two consecutive zeros $x_1<x_2$ on the real axis.

On $(x_1,x_2)$ the function $v=|u|$ is positive and smooth, and a calculation with the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives $v''\ge\operatorname{Re}(\overline u\,u'')/|u|$. Therefore
\[
v''\ \ge\ -|p|\,v\ \ge\ -\frac{v}{(1-x^2)^2}.
\]
We compare with $y(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, which is positive on $(-1,1)$ and satisfies $y''=-y/(1-x^2)^2$. The function $W=v'y-vy'$ has derivative $W'=v''y-vy''\ge0$. But the zeros of $u$ are simple, so that $W(x_1^+)=|u'(x_1)|\,y(x_1)>0$ and $W(x_2^-)=-|u'(x_2)|\,y(x_2)<0$. A nondecreasing function cannot pass from a positive value to a negative one, and this contradiction proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We write $z=(z_1,\dots,z_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n$, with Hermitian product $z\cdot w=\sum_iz_i\overline{w_i}$ and Euclidean norm $|z|=(z\cdot z)^{1/2}$. We shall also use the \emph{bilinear} product
\[
\langle a,v\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^na_iv_i,
\]
without conjugation, which is the one that appears when a holomorphic gradient acts on a vector, and the norm $|z|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|$. The unit ball and the polydisk are
\[
\mathbb{B}^n=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:\ |z|<1\},\qquad\mathbb{D}^n=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:\ |z|_\infty<1\}.
\]
We denote by $L^k(\mathbb{C}^n)$ the space of $k$-linear mappings from $(\mathbb{C}^n)^k$ into $\mathbb{C}^n$, with the norm $\|T\|=\sup\{|T(u_1,\dots,u_k)|:\ |u_j|=1\}$. For a matrix $A$, $\overline A$ is the matrix of conjugate entries, $A^t$ the transpose and $A^*=\overline A^{\,t}$ the adjoint.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:pfaltzgraff}
If $F\in\mathcal{LS}(\mathbb{B}^n)$ satisfies
\[
(1-|z|^2)\,\bigl\|DF(z)^{-1}D^2F(z)(z,\cdot)\bigr\|\le1,\qquad z\in\mathbb{B}^n,
\]
then $F$ is univalent in $\mathbb{B}^n$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:oda}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ be simply connected.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ is locally biholomorphic, the system \eqref{eq:sistema} with $P^k_{ij}=S^k_{ij}F$, $0\le k\le n$, is completely integrable and is in canonical form. The functions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base}
u_0=J_F^{-\frac{1}{n+1}},\qquad u_i=f_i\,J_F^{-\frac{1}{n+1}}\quad(i=1,\dots,n)
\end{equation}
form a basis of solutions, and $F=(u_1/u_0,\dots,u_n/u_0)$.
\item[(b)] Conversely, if \eqref{eq:sistema} is completely integrable and is in canonical form, and $u_0,\dots,u_n$ is a basis of solutions, then $F=(u_1/u_0,\dots,u_n/u_0)$ is locally biholomorphic where $u_0\ne0$, and $P^k_{ij}=S^k_{ij}F$ for $0\le k\le n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
(a) Let $u_0=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}$, which is a solution by \eqref{eq:S0}. For $u=f_lu_0$ we have
\[
\partial_{ij}u=u_0\,\partial_{ij}f_l+\partial_if_l\,\partial_ju_0+\partial_jf_l\,\partial_iu_0+f_l\,\partial_{ij}u_0 ,
\]
and since $u_0$ is a solution, $u$ will be one if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:clave}
u_0\,\partial_{ij}f_l+\partial_if_l\,\partial_ju_0+\partial_jf_l\,\partial_iu_0=u_0\sum_kS^k_{ij}F\,\partial_kf_l .
\end{equation}
Now $\sum_k\bigl[DF^{-1}D^2F(e_i,e_j)\bigr]_k\,\partial_kf_l=\partial_{ij}f_l$, so that by \eqref{eq:oda}
\[
\sum_kS^k_{ij}F\,\partial_kf_l=\partial_{ij}f_l-\frac{1}{n+1}\bigl(\partial_if_l\,\partial_j\log J_F+\partial_jf_l\,\partial_i\log J_F\bigr),
\]
and \eqref{eq:clave} follows from $\partial_ju_0=-\frac{1}{n+1}u_0\,\partial_j\log J_F$. The $n+1$ functions \eqref{eq:base} are linearly independent, since a relation $c_0+\sum c_if_i\equiv0$ gives, upon differentiation, $\sum c_i\nabla f_i=0$, and $DF$ is invertible. The solution space then has dimension $n+1$.

(b) Consider the determinant $W$ of the matrix of order $n+1$ whose rows are the vectors $(u_j,\nabla u_j)$, $j=0,\dots,n$. It does not vanish, because a solution is determined by its value and its gradient at a point. When $W$ is differentiated with respect to $z_i$ column by column, the column of the $u_j$ contributes nothing, and the column of the $\partial_mu_j$, replaced by means of \eqref{eq:sistema}, contributes $P^m_{im}W$. Thus $\partial_iW=\bigl(\sum_mP^m_{im}\bigr)W=0$ by \eqref{eq:canonica}, and $W$ is constant. On the other hand, writing $u_j=u_0f_j$ and subtracting from each row a multiple of the first, we obtain $W=u_0^{\,n+1}J_F$. Consequently $J_F\ne0$ and $u_0=c\,J_F^{-1/(n+1)}$ with $c$ constant. By part (a), the system associated with $F$ has as solutions $J_F^{-1/(n+1)}(1,f_1,\dots,f_n)$, that is, the multiples of $u_0,\dots,u_n$. The two systems have the same solution space, and a completely integrable system is determined by it. At each point the vectors $(u(z),\nabla u(z))$, with $u$ a solution, fill $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$, and \eqref{eq:sistema} expresses the Hessian as a linear function of that vector. The coefficients coincide.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:mobius}
If $M$ is a Möbius transformation, $S^k_{ij}(M\circ F)=S^k_{ij}F$ for $0\le k\le n$. Moreover, for $n\ge2$,
\[
S^k_{ij}F\equiv0\ \text{ for all }i,j,k\ge1\iff F\ \text{is a Möbius transformation.}
\]
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The systems associated with $F$ and with $M\circ F$ have the same solution space, hence the same coefficients. For $F(z)=z$ all the coefficients vanish, and therefore they also vanish for every Möbius transformation. Conversely, suppose $S^k_{ij}F=0$ for $k\ge1$, so that the system is $\partial_{ij}u=S^0_{ij}F\,u$. Equating $\partial_k(\partial_{ij}u)$ with $\partial_j(\partial_{ik}u)$ for an index $k\ne j$, which is possible because $n\ge2$, and comparing the coefficients of $\partial_ku$, which at a given point is arbitrary, we obtain $S^0_{ij}F=0$. The system then reduces to $\operatorname{Hess} u=0$, its solutions are the affine functions, and $F$ is a quotient of affine functions.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:soluciones}
Every nontrivial solution $u$ of the system associated with $F$ is of the form $u=J_G^{-1/(n+1)}$ with $G=T\circ F$ and $T$ a Möbius transformation. The mapping $G$ is holomorphic off the zero set of $u$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- obs-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:n1}
For $n=1$ formula \eqref{eq:oda} gives $S^1_{11}f=f''/f'-f''/f'=0$ for every $f$, and the system reduces to $u''=S^0_{11}f\,u$ with $u_0=(f')^{-1/2}$. Therefore
\[
S^0_{11}f=-\tfrac12\,Sf .
\]
The classical Schwarzian is the coefficient of \emph{order zero}, an operator of third order. For $n\ge2$ the situation is reversed. The $S^k_{ij}F$ with $k\ge1$ are operators of second order, nontrivial, and it is they that characterize the Möbius transformations. The $S^0_{ij}F$ are no longer free data. The equality of the mixed derivatives $\partial_k(\partial_{ij}u)=\partial_j(\partial_{ik}u)$ determines them in terms of the former \cite{H07}, through the formulas
\begin{align}
S^0_{ii}F&=\frac{1}{n-1}\Bigl[\sum_{j,k=1}^nS^k_{ij}F\,S^j_{ki}F-\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\partial }{\partial z_k}S^k_{ii}F\Bigr],\label{eq:S0ii}\\
S^0_{ij}F&=\frac{\partial }{\partial z_j}S^i_{ii}F-\frac{\partial }{\partial z_i}S^i_{ij}F+\sum_{k=1}^n\bigl(S^k_{ii}F\,S^i_{kj}F-S^k_{ij}F\,S^i_{ki}F\bigr),\qquad j\ne i.\label{eq:S0ij}
\end{align}
                                                                                                       
The factor $1/(n-1)$ shows why the case $n=1$ is excluded. For $n=1$ there are no equations of second order, the only second derivative remains free, and an operator of third order is needed; this is the case of equality in \eqref{eq:recuento}. In several variables, by contrast, the information lies in an object of second order, closer to a pre-Schwarzian than to a Schwarzian, and this will have to be kept in mind when interpreting the norms.
<!-- end obs-1 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{def:operador}
The \emph{Schwarzian operator} of $F$ at $z$ is the symmetric bilinear mapping
\[
S_F(z)(v,w)=\bigl(v^tS^1F(z)w,\dots,v^tS^nF(z)w\bigr),\qquad v,w\in\mathbb{C}^n .
\]
We also set $S^0_F(z)(v,w)=v^tS^0F(z)w$, with scalar values.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:producto}
Let $F(z)=(f(z_1),z_2,\dots,z_n)$ with $f'\ne0$. Then $J_F=f'(z_1)$ and \eqref{eq:SP} gives
\[
S^1_{11}F=\frac{n-1}{n+1}\,\frac{f''}{f'}(z_1),\qquad S^i_{1i}F=-\frac{1}{n+1}\,\frac{f''}{f'}(z_1)\quad(i\ge2),
\]
and the remaining coefficients vanish. Here the operator $S_F$ records the pre-Schwarzian of $f$ and not its Schwarzian.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:RS}
The extension operator of Roper and Suffridge \cite{RS} associates with a locally univalent function $f$ of the disk, with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$, the mapping
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RS}
\Phi_f(z)=\bigl(f(z_1),\sqrt{f'(z_1)}\,z_2,\dots,\sqrt{f'(z_1)}\,z_n\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here $J_{\Phi_f}=(f')^{(n+1)/2}$, and a computation with \eqref{eq:SP} shows that the only nonzero coefficients are
\[
S^k_{11}\Phi_f(z)=\tfrac12\,z_k\,Sf(z_1),\qquad k=2,\dots,n.
\]
Now the classical Schwarzian does appear, and $S_{\Phi_f}\equiv0$ exactly when $f$ is a Möbius transformation.
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:curvatura}
Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic, $n\ge2$, and let $\Sigma=F^{-1}(H)$ be as in \eqref{eq:Sigma}. For every $z\in\Sigma$ and every unit vector $v$ tangent to $\Sigma$ at $z$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:curvatura}
\kappa_\Sigma(z,v)=\frac{\bigl|\langle \nabla u(z),S_F(z)(v,v)\rangle\bigr|}{|\nabla u(z)|} .
\end{equation}
That is, $\kappa_\Sigma(z,v)$ is the modulus of the component of $S_F(z)(v,v)$ in the normal direction $N(z)$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:curvaturacota}
\kappa_\Sigma(z,v)\le|S_F(z)(v,v)| .
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since $u$ is holomorphic and vanishes along $\gamma$, differentiating $u(\gamma(t))=0$ twice we obtain
\[
\langle \nabla u(\gamma),\gamma'\rangle=0,\qquad\operatorname{Hess} u(\gamma)(\gamma',\gamma')+\langle \nabla u(\gamma),\gamma''\rangle=0 .
\]
The acceleration of a geodesic is normal to the surface, so that $\gamma''(0)=c\,N(z)$ with $c\in\mathbb{C}$, and then $\langle \nabla u(z),\gamma''(0)\rangle=c\,|\nabla u(z)|$. Therefore
\[
\kappa_\Sigma(z,v)=|c|=\frac{|\operatorname{Hess} u(z)(v,v)|}{|\nabla u(z)|} .
\]
On the other hand $u(z)=0$, and the system \eqref{eq:sistemacompacto} reduces at that point to $\operatorname{Hess} u(z)(v,v)=\langle \nabla u(z),S_F(z)(v,v)\rangle$. This proves \eqref{eq:curvatura}, and \eqref{eq:curvaturacota} is the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:modv}
Let $n\ge2$ and let $Q:\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be bilinear and symmetric, with coefficients $Q^k_{ij}$ such that $\sum_jQ^j_{ij}=0$ for all $i$. If $Q(v,v)$ is a multiple of $v$ for every $v\in\mathbb{C}^n$, then $Q=0$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Write $Q^k(v)$ for the $k$-th component of $Q(v,v)$, which is a homogeneous polynomial of degree two. The hypothesis is equivalent to $Q^k(v)\,v_i=Q^i(v)\,v_k$ for all $i,k$. If $i\ne k$, the polynomial $v_k$ divides $Q^k(v)\,v_i$ and therefore $Q^k(v)$, so that $Q^k(v)=\ell_k(v)\,v_k$ with $\ell_k$ linear; substituting, $\ell_k=\ell_i$. Thus $Q(v,v)=\ell(v)\,v$ with $\ell(v)=\sum_i\ell_iv_i$, and by polarization $Q^k_{ij}=\tfrac12(\ell_i\delta^k_j+\ell_j\delta^k_i)$. Then $\sum_jQ^j_{ij}=\tfrac12(n+1)\ell_i$, and the hypothesis on the trace gives $\ell=0$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:curvatura}
Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic, $n\ge2$, and $z\in\Omega$. Then $S_F(z)=0$ if and only if every preimage of a hyperplane that passes through $z$ has zero extrinsic curvature at $z$, in all tangent directions. Consequently, $F$ is a Möbius transformation if and only if the preimages of the hyperplanes are totally geodesic.
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If the curvatures vanish, \eqref{eq:curvmax} says that $S_F(z)(v,v)$ is a multiple of $v$ for every $v$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:modv} applies to $Q=S_F(z)$, which is trace-free by \eqref{eq:canonica}. The converse is \eqref{eq:curvaturacota}, and the last assertion follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:mobius}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:halley}
Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic in a simply connected domain, with $F(a)=0$. Then
\[
G(a)=a,\qquad DG(a)=0,\qquad D^2G(a)=S_F(a).
\]
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
From \eqref{eq:producto}, $DG(z)(v)=Dg(z)^{-1}D^2g(z)\bigl(v,Dg(z)^{-1}g(z)\bigr)$, which vanishes at $a$ because $g(a)=0$. Differentiating once more and evaluating at $a$, the terms that contain $g(a)$ disappear and we are left with $D^2G(a)=Dg(a)^{-1}D^2g(a)=P_g(a)$. On the other hand, at $a$ we have $Dg=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}DF$ and
\[
D^2g(v,w)=J_F^{-\frac{1}{n+1}}\Bigl[D^2F(v,w)-\frac{1}{n+1}\bigl(\langle \nabla\log J_F,v\rangle\,DF\,w+\langle \nabla\log J_F,w\rangle\,DF\,v\bigr)\Bigr],
\]
whence $P_g(a)=S_F(a)$ by \eqref{eq:SP}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:unicidad}
Let $f,g$ be locally biholomorphic in a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^n$. Then $P_f=P_g$ if and only if $f=Ag+b$ with $A$ a constant invertible matrix and $b\in\mathbb{C}^n$.
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For $n=1$ it suffices to integrate twice. Let $n\ge2$. If $P_f=P_g$, taking traces and using \eqref{eq:jacobi} we obtain $\nabla\log J_f=\nabla\log J_g$, and then $S_f=S_g$ by \eqref{eq:SP}. The coefficients of order zero also coincide, by Remark~\ref{obs:n1}, and the systems associated with $f$ and with $g$ are the same. By Theorem~\ref{thm:oda}, $f=T\circ g$ with $T$ a Möbius transformation. Since $J_f=(J_T\circ g)\,J_g$ and $J_f/J_g$ is constant, $J_T$ is constant, and by \eqref{eq:jacmobius} $T$ is affine. The converse is immediate.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:prescribir}
Let $A(z)=(a^k_{ij}(z))$ be a holomorphic bilinear operator in a simply connected domain $\Omega$. There exists a locally biholomorphic $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ with $P_f=A$ if and only if
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $a^k_{ij}=a^k_{ji}$ for all $i,j,k$;
\item[(ii)] there exists $\phi$ holomorphic in $\Omega$ with $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^na^k_{kj}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z_j}$, $j=1,\dots,n$;
\item[(iii)] the system \eqref{eq:sistema} with coefficients $P^k_{ij}=a^k_{ij}-\frac{1}{n+1}\bigl(\delta^k_i\,\partial_j\phi+\delta^k_j\,\partial_i\phi\bigr)$ is completely integrable, and $\exp(-\phi/(n+1))$ is one of its solutions.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
\label{def:norma}
Let $\Omega$ be the ball or the polydisk, with its Bergman metric, and let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic. We define
\[
\|S_F(z)\|=\sup_{\|v\|_z=1}\|S_F(z)(v,v)\|_z,\qquad\|S_F\|=\sup_{z\in\Omega}\|S_F(z)\|.
\]
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:invariancia}
If $F:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ is locally biholomorphic and $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{B}^n)$, then $\|S_{F\circ\sigma}(z)\|=\|S_F(\sigma(z))\|$ for all $z\in\mathbb{B}^n$. In particular $\|S_{F\circ\sigma}\|=\|S_F\|$.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $\sigma$ is a Möbius transformation, \eqref{eq:precomp} holds. Let $w=D\sigma(z)v$. Since $\sigma$ is an isometry, $\|w\|_{\sigma(z)}=\|v\|_z$ and
\[
\|S_{F\circ\sigma}(z)(v,v)\|_z=\|D\sigma(z)^{-1}S_F(\sigma(z))(w,w)\|_z=\|S_F(\sigma(z))(w,w)\|_{\sigma(z)}.
\]
It suffices to take the supremum over $\|v\|_z=1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- obs-2: body_md -->
\label{obs:curvaturabergman}
The Bergman norm controls the curvatures of Theorem~\ref{thm:curvatura}. By \eqref{eq:bergmanbola},
\[
\frac{(n+1)\,|v|^2}{1-|z|^2}\ \le\ \|v\|_z^2\ \le\ \frac{(n+1)\,|v|^2}{(1-|z|^2)^2},
\]
and applying the first inequality to $S_F(z)(v,v)$ and the second to $v$ we obtain, for $|v|=1$,
\[
|S_F(z)(v,v)|\le\frac{\sqrt{1-|z|^2}}{\sqrt{n+1}}\,\|S_F(z)\|\,\|v\|_z^2\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,\|S_F(z)\|}{(1-|z|^2)^{3/2}} .
\]
By \eqref{eq:curvaturacota}, if $\|S_F\|\le\alpha$ in $\mathbb{B}^n$ then every preimage $\Sigma$ of a hyperplane satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:curvaturabergman}
\kappa_\Sigma(z,v)\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha}{(1-|z|^2)^{3/2}},\qquad z\in\Sigma .
\end{equation}
At the origin the two inequalities used are equalities.
<!-- end obs-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:cotas}
Let $F:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\|S_F\|\le\alpha$, let $z=(z_1,0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{B}^n$ and $\tau=1-|z_1|^2$. For indices $i,j,k\ge2$, with $i\ne j$ wherever both appear,
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
|S^1_{11}F(z)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-1}, & |S^k_{11}F(z)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-3/2},\\[4pt]
|S^1_{1j}F(z)|\le2\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-1/2}, & |S^k_{1j}F(z)|\le2\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-1},\\[4pt]
|S^1_{ii}F(z)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha, & |S^k_{ii}F(z)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-1/2},\\[4pt]
|S^1_{ij}F(z)|\le2\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha, & |S^k_{ij}F(z)|\le2\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,\tau^{-1/2}.
\end{array}
\]
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:normal}
For each $\alpha<\infty$ the family $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ is normal and compact in the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:ordennorma}
\[
\|\operatorname{ord}\|\,\mathcal{F}_\alpha\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}}{2}\,\alpha+\frac{2}{n+1}\,\operatorname{ord}\mathcal{F}_\alpha .
\]
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $F\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ and $|v|=1$. At the origin $J_F(0)=1$ and $P_F(0)=D^2F(0)=2A_2$, so that \eqref{eq:SP} reads
\[
2A_2(v,v)=S_F(0)(v,v)+\frac{2}{n+1}\,\langle \nabla J_F(0),v\rangle\,v .
\]
The Bergman metric at the origin is $(n+1)$ times the Euclidean metric. Therefore $v/\sqrt{n+1}$ is a unit vector for it, and the hypothesis $\|S_F(0)\|\le\alpha$ says that $|S_F(0)(v,v)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha$. Consequently
\[
|A_2(v,v)|\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}}{2}\,\alpha+\frac{1}{n+1}\,|\nabla J_F(0)|,
\]
and $|\nabla J_F(0)|\le2\,\operatorname{ord}\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ by \eqref{eq:orden}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:expansion}
Let $F$ be locally biholomorphic near the origin, with $J_F(0)=1$ and $\nabla J_F(0)=\Lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$. Then
\[
\frac{\nabla J_F}{J_F}(\zeta)=\Lambda+A\,\zeta+O(|\zeta|^2),\qquad\zeta\to0,
\]
where $A=(A_{ij})$ is the symmetric matrix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:matrizA}
A_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^nS^k_{ij}F(0)\,\lambda_k-(n+1)\,S^0_{ij}F(0)+\frac{\lambda_i\lambda_j}{n+1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $u_0=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}$, so that $\partial_i\log J_F=-(n+1)\,\partial_iu_0/u_0$. Since $u_0(0)=1$,
\[
\partial_j\Bigl(\frac{\partial_iu_0}{u_0}\Bigr)(0)=\partial_{ij}u_0(0)-\partial_iu_0(0)\,\partial_ju_0(0).
\]
Now $\nabla u_0(0)=-\Lambda/(n+1)$, and $u_0$ is a solution of the system \eqref{eq:sistema} associated with $F$, hence
\[
\partial_{ij}u_0(0)=-\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_kS^k_{ij}F(0)\,\lambda_k+S^0_{ij}F(0).
\]
Multiplying by $-(n+1)$ we obtain \eqref{eq:matrizA}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:automorfismo}
For each $\zeta\in\mathbb{B}^n$ there exists $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{B}^n)$ with $\sigma(0)=\zeta$ such that
\[
D\sigma(0)=I+O(|\zeta|^2),\qquad\frac{\nabla J_\sigma}{J_\sigma}(0)=-(n+1)\,\overline{\zeta}.
\]
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
If $\zeta=(\zeta_1,0,\dots,0)$ we take
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigma}
\sigma(z)=\Bigl(\frac{z_1+\zeta_1}{1+\overline{\zeta_1}z_1},\ \frac{\sqrt{1-|\zeta_1|^2}\;z_2}{1+\overline{\zeta_1}z_1},\ \dots,\ \frac{\sqrt{1-|\zeta_1|^2}\;z_n}{1+\overline{\zeta_1}z_1}\Bigr),
\end{equation}
for which
\[
J_\sigma(z)=\frac{(1-|\zeta_1|^2)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}}{(1+\overline{\zeta_1}z_1)^{n+1}},\qquad D\sigma(0)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(1-|\zeta_1|^2,\sqrt{1-|\zeta_1|^2},\dots,\sqrt{1-|\zeta_1|^2}\bigr).
\]
The general case is obtained by conjugating with a unitary rotation.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:caracteristica}
Let $F_0\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ be extremal for $A_\alpha$, and suppose, after a rotation, that $\nabla J_{F_0}(0)=(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$ with $\lambda=A_\alpha>0$. Then, at the origin,
\begin{align}
&\lambda^2+(n+1)\,S^1_{11}F_0\,\lambda-(n+1)^2S^0_{11}F_0-(n+1)^2=0,\label{eq:carac1}\\
&S^1_{1j}F_0\,\lambda-(n+1)\,S^0_{1j}F_0=0,\qquad j=2,\dots,n.\label{eq:carac2}
\end{align}
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\zeta\in\mathbb{B}^n$ be small, $\sigma$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:automorfismo} and $G=\Lambda_\sigma(F_0)\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$. From \eqref{eq:koebe},
\[
J_G(z)=J_\sigma(0)^{-1}J_{F_0}(\zeta)^{-1}\,J_{F_0}(\sigma(z))\,J_\sigma(z),
\]
and differentiating logarithmically at $z=0$, with the two lemmas,
\[
\nabla J_G(0)=\frac{\nabla J_{F_0}}{J_{F_0}}(\zeta)\,D\sigma(0)+\frac{\nabla J_\sigma}{J_\sigma}(0)=\Lambda+A\,\zeta-(n+1)\,\overline\zeta+O(|\zeta|^2),
\]
with $\Lambda=(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$. Only the first component contributes to the modulus to first order, and we find
\[
|\nabla J_G(0)|^2=\lambda^2+2\lambda\,\operatorname{Re}\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^nA_{1j}\zeta_j-(n+1)\,\zeta_1\Bigr]+O(|\zeta|^2).
\]
Since $F_0$ is extremal, the left-hand side does not exceed $\lambda^2$. The real part of a linear form in $\zeta$ that is less than or equal to $O(|\zeta|^2)$ for all small $\zeta$ vanishes identically, and therefore
\[
A_{11}=n+1,\qquad A_{1j}=0\quad(j\ge2).
\]
With $\Lambda=(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$, formula \eqref{eq:matrizA} gives $A_{1j}=S^1_{1j}\lambda-(n+1)S^0_{1j}+\delta_{1j}\lambda^2/(n+1)$, and the two preceding relations are \eqref{eq:carac1} and \eqref{eq:carac2}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:ordensup}
\[
\operatorname{ord}\mathcal{F}_\alpha\le\frac{n+1}{2}\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{n+1}}{2}\,\alpha+\sqrt{1+\frac{n+1}{4}\,\alpha^2+C(n,\alpha)}\Bigr),
\]
with $C(n,\alpha)$ as in \eqref{eq:Cnalpha}.
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Completing the square in \eqref{eq:carac1},
\[
\Bigl(\lambda+\tfrac12(n+1)S^1_{11}\Bigr)^2=(n+1)^2\Bigl(1+\tfrac14(S^1_{11})^2+S^0_{11}\Bigr),
\]
and it suffices to use $|S^1_{11}F_0(0)|\le\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha$ and $|S^0_{11}F_0(0)|\le C(n,\alpha)$, which are Lemma~\ref{lem:cotas} and \eqref{eq:cotasS0} at the origin.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:constantes}
If $F$ is locally biholomorphic in $\mathbb{B}^n$ and all the $S^k_{ij}F$, $k\ge1$, are constant, then $\|S_F\|=\|S_F(0)\|$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
From \eqref{eq:bergmanbola} and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, for every vector $w$
\[
\frac{(n+1)\,|w|^2}{1-|z|^2}\le\|w\|_z^2\le\frac{(n+1)\,|w|^2}{(1-|z|^2)^2}.
\]
If $\|v\|_z=1$, the first inequality gives $|v|^2\le(1-|z|^2)/(n+1)$, and the second, applied to $w=S_F(z)(v,v)$, which does not depend on $z$, gives
\[
\|S_F(z)(v,v)\|_z\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,|v|^2}{1-|z|^2}\,\Bigl|S_F\Bigl(\frac{v}{|v|},\frac{v}{|v|}\Bigr)\Bigr|\le\frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}}\,\sup_{|e|=1}|S_F(e,e)|=\|S_F(0)\| .\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:ordeninf}
For $n=2$ we have $\operatorname{ord}\mathcal{F}_\alpha\ge\tfrac94\alpha$, and for $n>2$,
\[
\operatorname{ord}\mathcal{F}_\alpha\ge\frac{(n+1)^{3/2}}{2(n-1)}\,\alpha .
\]
<!-- end thm-13 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\kappa=\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha/(n-1)$ and consider the system with constant coefficients
\[
S^1_{11}=-\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha,\qquad S^k_{1k}=\kappa\quad(k\ge2),
\]
with the remaining $S^k_{ij}$ equal to zero. It satisfies \eqref{eq:canonica}, and formulas \eqref{eq:S0ii}--\eqref{eq:S0ij} give $S^0_{11}=n\kappa^2$ and $S^0_{ij}=0$ in the remaining cases. The system reads
\[
u_{11}=-\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,u_1+n\kappa^2u,\qquad u_{1j}=\kappa\,u_j\quad(j\ge2),\qquad u_{ij}=0\quad(i,j\ge2),
\]
and it can be integrated by hand. Its solutions are the combinations of $e^{\kappa z_1}$, $e^{-n\kappa z_1}$ and $e^{\kappa z_1}z_j$, $j\ge2$. There are $n+1$ of them, and the system is completely integrable. The solution $u=e^{\kappa z_1}$ does not vanish, and has $u(0)=1$, $\nabla u(0)=(\kappa,0,\dots,0)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:oda}(b), applied to a basis of solutions whose first element is $u$, there is a mapping $G$ locally biholomorphic in $\mathbb{B}^n$, which we may normalize, with $J_G=u^{-(n+1)}$ and, therefore,
\[
|\nabla J_G(0)|=(n+1)\,\kappa=\frac{(n+1)^{3/2}}{n-1}\,\alpha .
\]
It remains to compute the norm. At the origin $S(v,v)=\bigl(-\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha\,v_1^2,\,2\kappa v_1v_2,\dots,2\kappa v_1v_n\bigr)$, and maximizing over the vectors of Bergman norm one we find $\|S(0)\|=\alpha$ if $n>2$ and $\|S(0)\|=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\alpha$ if $n=2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:constantes} this is the value of $\|S_G\|$. For $n>2$ this gives $G\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ and the stated bound. For $n=2$ it gives $G\in\mathcal F_\beta$ with $\beta=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\alpha$ and $|\nabla J_G(0)|=3\sqrt3\,\alpha=\tfrac92\beta$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:ceroscomunes}
Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic in a simply connected domain. Then $F$ is univalent if and only if there do not exist $n$ linearly independent solutions of the system \eqref{eq:sistema} associated with $F$ that have two common zeros in $\Omega$.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $V$ be the space of solutions, of dimension $n+1$, and for $a\in\Omega$ let $V_a=\{u\in V:\ u(a)=0\}$. Since $u_0=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}$ does not vanish, $V_a$ is a hyperplane of $V$. With the basis \eqref{eq:base}, $F(a)=F(b)$ if and only if the vectors $(u_0(a),\dots,u_n(a))$ and $(u_0(b),\dots,u_n(b))$ are proportional, that is, if and only if $V_a=V_b$. And $V_a=V_b$ with $a\ne b$ means precisely that there are $n$ independent solutions that vanish at $a$ and at $b$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- thm-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:H07}
Let $F:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic and such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\|S_F(z)\|\le\alpha$ for all $z\in\mathbb{B}^n$;
\item[(ii)] $\displaystyle\sup_{\|a\|_z=\|b\|_z=1}|a^tS^0F(z)b|\le\frac{k}{1-|z|^2}$ for all $z\in\mathbb{B}^n$.
\end{enumerate}
If
\[
2\sqrt{n(n+1)}\,\bigl(e^{\pi/2}+2n+1\bigr)\alpha+(n+1)k\le1,
\]
then $F$ is univalent in $\mathbb{B}^n$.
<!-- end thm-14 -->
<!-- thm-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:loewner}
Let $F\in\mathcal{LS}(\mathbb{B}^n)$ and let $p=\nabla\log J_F(z)$. If for all $z\in\mathbb{B}^n$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critloewner}
\frac{\|S_F(z)(z,\cdot)\|}{1-|z|^2}+\Bigl\|\frac{\langle p,z\rangle\,S_F(z)(z,\cdot)-\langle p,S_F(z)(z,z)\rangle\,I}{n+1}+S^0_F(z)(z,z)\,I\Bigr\|\le\frac{1}{(1-|z|^2)^2},
\end{equation}
then $F$ is univalent in $\mathbb{B}^n$.
<!-- end thm-15 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $u_0,u_1,\dots,u_n$ be the basis \eqref{eq:base} and $u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)$. We define
\[
f(z,t)=\frac{u(e^{-t}z)+(e^{2t}-1)\,Du(e^{-t}z)(e^{-t}z)}{u_0(e^{-t}z)+(e^{2t}-1)\langle \nabla u_0(e^{-t}z),e^{-t}z\rangle},\qquad t\ge0,
\]
which is the transcription to $\mathbb{C}^n$ of the chain used to prove Nehari's criterion, and satisfies $f(z,0)=F(z)$. Upon differentiating, the second derivatives of $u$ and of $u_0$ appear, and they are eliminated with \eqref{eq:sistemacompacto}. The result is that $f$ satisfies \eqref{eq:loewnerpde} with
\[
h(z,t)=\bigl[I-E(z,t)\bigr]^{-1}\bigl[I+E(z,t)\bigr]z,
\]
where $E(z,t)$ is a linear operator built from $S_F$, $S^0_F$ and $\nabla\log u_0$ evaluated at $e^{-t}z$. Hypothesis \eqref{eq:critloewner}, together with $1-e^{-2t}<1-|e^{-t}z|^2$, gives $\|E(z,t)\|<1$, and then $\operatorname{Re}(h(z,t)\cdot z)>0$. The theorem quoted in Section~\ref{sec:prelim} completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:jacconst}
If $F\in\mathcal{LS}(\mathbb{B}^n)$ has constant Jacobian and $(1-|z|^2)\|S_F(z)(z,\cdot)\|\le1$ in $\mathbb{B}^n$, then $F$ is univalent.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:rhoinv}
If $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{B}^n)$ and $F$ is locally biholomorphic in $\mathbb{B}^n$, then $\rho_{F\circ\sigma}=\rho_F\circ\sigma$.
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
This is a consequence of $J_{F\circ\sigma}=(J_F\circ\sigma)J_\sigma$ and of the identity
\[
|J_\sigma(z)|=\Bigl(\frac{1-|\sigma(z)|^2}{1-|z|^2}\Bigr)^{\frac{n+1}{2}},
\]
which for $\sigma$ of the form \eqref{eq:sigma} is verified directly and for unitary rotations is evident.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:radial}
Let $F\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ and let $u$ be a solution of the associated system that does not vanish in $\mathbb{B}^n$. Then $\varphi(x)=|u(x,0,\dots,0)|$ satisfies
\[
\varphi''(x)+\frac{\delta(n,\alpha)}{(1-x^2)^2}\,\varphi(x)\ge0,\qquad-1<x<1 .
\]
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:soluciones}, $u=J_G^{-1/(n+1)}$ with $G=T\circ F$ holomorphic in $\mathbb{B}^n$, and $\|S_G\|=\|S_F\|\le\alpha$. After an affine normalization, which only multiplies $u$ by a constant, we may assume that $G\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$; we write $F$ instead of $G$.

Fix $\zeta=(x,0,\dots,0)$, let $\sigma$ be the automorphism \eqref{eq:sigma} and $H=\Lambda_\sigma(F)\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$. Then $v=J_H^{-1/(n+1)}$ is a constant multiple of $(u\circ\sigma)\,w$, with $w=J_\sigma^{-1/(n+1)}$, and differentiating logarithmically at the origin,
\[
\frac{\nabla u}{u}(\zeta)\,D\sigma(0)=\frac{\nabla v}{v}(0)-\frac{\nabla w}{w}(0).
\]
The first term on the right is $-\nabla J_H(0)/(n+1)$, of norm at most $A_\alpha$, and the second is $\overline\zeta$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:automorfismo}. Recalling the form of $D\sigma(0)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gradiente}
(1-x^2)^2\,|\partial_1u(\zeta)|^2+(1-x^2)\sum_{k=2}^n|\partial_ku(\zeta)|^2\le(A_\alpha+1)^2\,|u(\zeta)|^2 .
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the vector $(1-x^2)e_1/\sqrt{n+1}$ is a unit vector for the Bergman metric at $\zeta$, and the hypothesis $\|S_F(\zeta)\|\le\alpha$ applied to it gives
\[
(1-x^2)^2\,|S^1_{11}F(\zeta)|^2+(1-x^2)^3\sum_{k=2}^n|S^k_{11}F(\zeta)|^2\le(n+1)\,\alpha^2 .
\]
From these two inequalities and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{k=1}^nS^k_{11}F(\zeta)\,\partial_ku(\zeta)\Bigr|\le\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,(A_\alpha+1)\,\alpha}{(1-x^2)^2}\,|u(\zeta)| .
\]
Finally, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:nehari},
\[
\varphi''\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{Re}(\overline u\,\partial_{11}u)}{|u|},\qquad\partial_{11}u=\sum_{k=1}^nS^k_{11}F\,\partial_ku+S^0_{11}F\,u .
\]
The first summand of $\partial_{11}u$ has just been estimated, and the second is controlled by \eqref{eq:cotasS0}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- thm-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:convexidad}
Let $F\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ with $\delta(n,\alpha)<1$, and let $u$ be a solution of the associated system that does not vanish in $\mathbb{B}^n$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hess}
\operatorname{Hess}_g\rho_u\ge\beta^2\rho_u\,g,\qquad\beta^2=\frac{1-\delta(n,\alpha)}{n+1},
\end{equation}
where $g$ is the Bergman metric and $\operatorname{Hess}_g$ is the Riemannian Hessian. In particular, $\rho_u$ is strictly convex along the geodesics of $g$, and it has at most one critical point in $\mathbb{B}^n$, which is then its absolute minimum.
<!-- end thm-16 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We must prove that $(\rho_u\circ\gamma)''\ge\beta^2\rho_u\circ\gamma$ for every geodesic $\gamma$ parametrized by arc length. Consider first the diameter $\gamma(t)=(x(t),0,\dots,0)$, for which $x'=(1-x^2)/\sqrt{n+1}$. With $\rho=\varphi\,(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ and $\varphi$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:radial},
\[
\frac{d\rho}{dt}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}}\Bigl[\varphi'\,(1-x^2)^{1/2}+x\,\varphi\,(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\Bigr],
\]
and differentiating once more the terms in $\varphi'$ cancel, and we are left with
\[
\frac{d^2\rho}{dt^2}=\frac{1-x^2}{n+1}\Bigl[\varphi''\,(1-x^2)^{1/2}+\varphi\,(1-x^2)^{-3/2}\Bigr]\ge\frac{1-\delta}{n+1}\cdot\frac{\varphi}{(1-x^2)^{1/2}}=\beta^2\rho .
\]
An arbitrary geodesic is the image of the diameter under an automorphism $\sigma$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:rhoinv}, $\rho_u\circ\sigma$ is a constant multiple of the density of a solution, which does not vanish either, of the system associated with the Koebe transform $\Lambda_\sigma(F)\in\mathcal{F}_\alpha$, and the preceding argument applies. A function that is strictly convex along geodesics, in a space in which any two points are joined by a geodesic, has at most one critical point.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:subbola}
Let $F\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_0}$ and let $u$ be a solution of the associated system that does not vanish in $B_r$. Then $\rho_{u,B_r}$ is convex with respect to the Bergman metric of the ball $B_r$.
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- thm-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:nocerosbola}
Let $F\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_0}$, and let $u$ be the solution of the associated system with $u(0)=1$, $\nabla u(0)=0$. Then $u$ does not vanish in $\mathbb{B}^n$, and
\[
|u(z)|\ge\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\,\cosh\bigl(\beta\,d(0,z)\bigr),\qquad d(0,z)=\frac{\sqrt{n+1}}{2}\log\frac{1+|z|}{1-|z|},
\]
where $d$ is the Bergman distance.
<!-- end thm-17 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $s\le1$ be the supremum of the Euclidean radii of the balls centered at the origin in which $u$ does not vanish, and suppose $s<1$. Then $u(z_1)=0$ for some $z_1$ with $|z_1|=s$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:subbola}, $\rho_{u,B_r}$ is convex in $B_r=\{|z|<s\}$, and since $\nabla u(0)=0$, the origin is a critical point and therefore a minimum. Thus
\[
|u(z)|\ge\frac1s\sqrt{s^2-|z|^2},\qquad|z|<s .
\]
As $z\to z_1$ along the radius, the left-hand side is $O(s-|z|)$ and the right-hand side is comparable to $\sqrt{s-|z|}$, which is absurd. Hence $s=1$. Now Theorem~\ref{thm:convexidad} applies to $u$. Along each geodesic through the origin, $\rho=\rho_u$ satisfies $\rho''\ge\beta^2\rho$, $\rho(0)=1$, $\rho'(0)=0$, and by comparison $\rho\ge\cosh(\beta t)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- thm-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:univCH15}
Every $F\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_0}$ is univalent in $\mathbb{B}^n$.
<!-- end thm-18 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Suppose that $F$ is not injective. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ceroscomunes} there are $n$ linearly independent solutions $u_1,\dots,u_n$ of the associated system that vanish at two distinct points, and by the linear invariance of the family we may assume that these points are the origin and $p=(a,0,\dots,0)$ with $0<a<1$. The gradients $\nabla u_i(0)$ are linearly independent, because a solution that vanishes at the origin together with its gradient is identically zero. Hence there is a linear combination $u$ with $\nabla u(0)=(1,0,\dots,0)$. Its zero set $\Sigma$ is a smooth complex hypersurface that passes through the origin and through $p$, and whose tangent plane at the origin is $\{z_1=0\}$.

For $0<b<1$ let $B^b$ be the Bergman ball with center $(b,0,\dots,0)$ whose boundary passes through the origin. Writing $z=(z_1,z')$, it is the set
\[
B^b=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb{B}^n:\ |1-bz_1|^2<1-|z|^2\bigr\}=\bigl\{2b\,\operatorname{Re} z_1>b^2|z_1|^2+|z|^2\bigr\}.
\]
These balls increase with $b$, they are all tangent to $\{z_1=0\}$ at the origin, and $p\in B^b$ as soon as $2b>a(1+b^2)$, which happens for $b$ close to $1$.

We compare $\Sigma$ with these balls near the origin. There $\Sigma$ is a graph $z_1=\phi(z')$ with $\phi$ holomorphic, $\phi(0)=0$ and $\nabla\phi(0)=0$, and its extrinsic curvature at the origin, in the direction $(0,v')$, is $|\operatorname{Hess}\phi(0)(v',v')|$. By \eqref{eq:curvaturabergman} this curvature does not exceed $\sqrt{n+1}\,\alpha_0$, which is less than $1$ because $\delta(n,\alpha_0)<1$. Hence there are a neighborhood $U$ of the origin and a constant $c<\tfrac12$ such that $|\phi(z')|\le c\,|z'|^2$ on $\Sigma\cap U$. If a point of $\Sigma\cap U$ were in the closure of some $B^b$, we would have $|z'|^2\le2b\,\operatorname{Re}\phi(z')\le2c\,|z'|^2$, and therefore $z'=0$. Thus, inside $U$, the hypersurface $\Sigma$ meets the closures of all the balls $B^b$ only at the origin. In particular $u$ does not vanish in $B^b$ when $b$ is small.

Let $b_1$ be the supremum of the $b$ such that $u$ does not vanish in $B^b$. If $b_1=1$ we have a contradiction, because $u(p)=0$ and $p$ belongs to $B^b$ for $b$ close to $1$. Suppose then that $b_1<1$ and let $B_1=B^{b_1}$. The solution $u$ does not vanish in $B_1$, and it has zeros in $B^b$ for every $b>b_1$. These zeros lie outside $U$, and a limit point of them as $b\to b_1$ is a point $z_2$ of the boundary of $B_1$, different from the origin, with $u(z_2)=0$.

The density $\rho_{u,B_1}$ is convex with respect to the Bergman metric of $B_1$. The geodesic of this metric that joins the boundary points $0$ and $z_2$ reaches them transversally. Near each of them, $|u|$ is at most proportional to the distance to the point, while the denominator of $\rho_{u,B_1}$ is comparable to the square root of that distance. Hence $\rho_{u,B_1}$ tends to zero at both ends of the geodesic. But a positive convex function on the whole line cannot tend to zero at both ends. This contradiction proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- obs-3: body_md -->
\label{obs:univdirecta}
Once it is known that the solutions $u_{z_0}$ do not vanish, univalence can also be deduced without auxiliary balls. Suppose $F(a)=F(b)$ with $a\ne b$, and let $u_a$, $u_b$ be the solutions constructed before the theorem. By Theorem~\ref{thm:convexidad} the density $\rho_{u_a}$ has its unique minimum at $a$ and $\rho_{u_b}$ has it at $b$, so that
\[
\rho_{u_a}(a)<\rho_{u_a}(b),\qquad\rho_{u_b}(b)<\rho_{u_b}(a).
\]
But $u_a=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}\,l_a(F)$ and $u_b=J_F^{-1/(n+1)}\,l_b(F)$ with $l_a,l_b$ affine functions. The quotient $u_a/u_b=l_a(F)/l_b(F)$ depends only on the value of $F$ and takes the same value at $a$ and at $b$, and then
\[
\frac{\rho_{u_a}(a)}{\rho_{u_b}(a)}=\frac{\rho_{u_a}(b)}{\rho_{u_b}(b)},
\]
which contradicts the two preceding inequalities. The same argument shows that the hyperplanes $H(z_0)$ are distinct for distinct points $z_0$.
<!-- end obs-3 -->
<!-- thm-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:distorsion}
If $F\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_0}$ is normalized, then
\[
|J_F(z)|\le\frac{2^{n+1}}{(1-|z|)^{\mu}},\qquad\mu=\frac{n+1}{2}\bigl(1-\beta\sqrt{n+1}\bigr).
\]
If in addition $F$ is quasiregular, $\|DF(z)\|\le C\,(1-|z|)^{-\mu/n}$, and in particular $F(\mathbb{B}^n)$ is bounded and $F$ has a continuous extension, in fact a Hölder continuous one, to $\overline{\mathbb{B}^n}$.
<!-- end thm-19 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
In this case the normalized solution is $J_F^{-1/(n+1)}$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:nocerosbola} gives
\[
\frac{|J_F(z)|^{-\frac{1}{n+1}}}{\sqrt{1-|z|^2}}\ge\cosh\bigl(\beta\,d(0,z)\bigr)\ge\frac12\Bigl(\frac{1}{1-|z|}\Bigr)^{\frac{\beta\sqrt{n+1}}{2}} ,
\]
from which the first bound follows. If $F$ is quasiregular, $\|DF\|^n$ is comparable to $|J_F|$, and since $\mu/n<1$ the resulting bound is integrable along the radii.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- thm-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:AW}
Let $F\in\mathcal F_{\alpha_0}$, with $\alpha_0$ as just indicated.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $F(\mathbb{B}^n)$ is a weakly linearly convex domain.
\item[(b)] If in addition $F$ is normalized and quasiregular, its continuous extension to $\overline{\mathbb{B}^n}$ is injective; the hyperplanes $H(z_0)$ are disjoint from $F(\overline{\mathbb{B}^n})$; and as $z_0\to\xi\in\partial\mathbb{B}^n$, $H(z_0)$ accumulates on hyperplanes that pass through $F(\xi)$.
\item[(c)] In the situation of \textup{(b)}, the mapping
\[
E_F(z)=\begin{cases}F(z),&|z|\le1,\\ H(z^*),&|z|>1,\end{cases}\qquad z^*=z/|z|^2,
\]
is injective and continuous. It assigns distinct hyperplanes to distinct points of the exterior, and it glues $F(\mathbb{B}^n)$ to a complementary domain in the projective dual of $\mathbb{C}^n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-20 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:poli}
If $F:\mathbb{D}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ is locally biholomorphic with $\|S_F\|\le\alpha<\infty$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cotapoli}
|S^k_{ij}F(z)|\le\frac{\sqrt2\,\alpha\,(1-|z_k|^2)}{(1-|z_i|^2)(1-|z_j|^2)},\qquad z\in\mathbb{D}^n,
\end{equation}
and consequently $S^k_{ij}F\equiv0$ whenever $k\ne i$ and $k\ne j$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The inequality is obtained by evaluating $S_F(z)$ on the unit vectors $2^{-1/2}(1-|z_i|^2)e_i$, and polarizing when $i\ne j$. If $k\ne i,j$, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:cotapoli} tends to zero as $|z_k|\to1$ with the other variables fixed; since $S^k_{ij}F$ is holomorphic in $z_k$, the maximum principle gives $S^k_{ij}F\equiv0$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- thm-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:poli}
Let $n\ge2$ and let $F:\mathbb{D}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be locally biholomorphic. If
\[
\|S_F\|\le\frac{1}{3\sqrt2},
\]
then $F$ is univalent in $\mathbb{D}^n$.
<!-- end thm-21 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Suppose $F(\xi)=F(\zeta)$ with $\xi_1\ne\zeta_1$, and normalize $F(\xi)=0$, $DF(\xi)=I$. Using \eqref{eq:estructura} and the relations between components, one shows inductively that $f(w)=f_1(w,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n)$ is locally injective in $\mathbb{D}$ and has $f(\xi_1)=f(\zeta_1)=0$. At the points $(w,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n)$ the differential $DF$ is diagonal and, after composing with a suitable Möbius transformation to make $\partial^2f_2/\partial z_1\partial z_2$ vanish along that line, we find
\[
\frac{f''}{f'}(w)=S^1_{11}F-2\,S^2_{12}F .
\]
By \eqref{eq:cotapoli}, $|f''/f'|\le3\sqrt2\,\alpha\,(1-|w|^2)^{-1}\le(1-|w|^2)^{-1}$. Becker's criterion says that $f$ is injective, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- thm-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:noceros}
Let \eqref{eq:sistema} be a completely integrable system in canonical form in $\mathbb{D}^n$ whose associated Schwarzian has norm at most $\alpha$, and let $u$ be the solution with $u(0)=1$, $\nabla u(0)=0$. If
\[
n\sqrt n\,\alpha\le\frac{1}{6.1},
\]
then $u$ does not vanish in $\mathbb{D}^n$, and
\[
\bigl(1-|z|_\infty^2\bigr)^{\sqrt n/2}\le|u(z)|\le\bigl(1-|z|_\infty^2\bigr)^{-\sqrt n/2}.
\]
<!-- end thm-22 -->
<!-- thm-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:convexaspoli}
Let $n\ge2$ and let $F:\mathbb{D}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ be a convex biholomorphic mapping.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] If $n>2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cotaconvexa}
\|S_F\|\le\frac{\sqrt{8(n+3)(n-1)}}{n+1}<2\sqrt2 .
\end{equation}
\item[(b)] If $n=2$, then $\|S_F\|\le2$, and the constant $2$ cannot be improved.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-23 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
For each fixed $x$, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:normaconvexa} is a convex function of $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, since it is a sum of squares of moduli of linear forms. Its maximum over the closed polydisk $\{|p_k|\le4\}$ is therefore attained when $|p_k|=4$ for all $k$. If $p_k=4e^{i\theta_k}$, the change $x_k\mapsto e^{i\theta_k}x_k$ preserves the unit sphere and removes the phases. Therefore $\|S_F\|\le\gamma_n$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lambda}
\gamma_n=2\sqrt2\ \max_{x\in\mathbb{C}^n,\ |x|=1}\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n|x_k|^2\,\Bigl|x_k-\frac{2}{n+1}\sum_{j=1}^nx_j\Bigr|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}

For (a) it suffices to bound $\gamma_n$, and the estimate, which holds for all $n\ge2$, is that of \cite{H26}. The sum in \eqref{eq:Lambda} does not exceed the largest of the factors $\bigl|x_k-\frac{2}{n+1}\sum_jx_j\bigr|^2$, because $\sum_k|x_k|^2=1$, and by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
\[
\Bigl|x_k-\frac{2}{n+1}\sum_jx_j\Bigr|^2\le\Bigl(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\Bigr)^2+(n-1)\Bigl(\frac{2}{n+1}\Bigr)^2=\frac{(n-1)(n+3)}{(n+1)^2}.
\]

For $n=2$ the maximum in \eqref{eq:Lambda} can be computed exactly, and it gives a smaller constant. Write $a=|x_1|$, $b=|x_2|$, $t=ab\in[0,\tfrac12]$. Since $x_1-\tfrac23(x_1+x_2)=\tfrac13(x_1-2x_2)$,
\[
\sum_k|x_k|^2\Bigl|x_k-\tfrac23(x_1+x_2)\Bigr|^2\le\frac19\bigl[a^2(a+2b)^2+b^2(b+2a)^2\bigr]=\frac19\bigl(1+4t+6t^2\bigr)\le\frac12,
\]
with equality for $x=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$. Hence $\gamma_2=2\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=2$ and $\|S_F\|\le2$. To see that the constant cannot be improved we take $\varphi_1(\zeta)=\varphi_2(\zeta)=\zeta/(1-\zeta)$ and $z=(r,r)$ with $0<r<1$. Then $p_1=p_2=2(1+r)\to4$ as $r\to1$, and by \eqref{eq:normaconvexa} $\|S_F(z)\|\to\gamma_2=2$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- thm-24: body_md -->
\label{thm:RSbola}
Let $\varphi$ be locally univalent in $\mathbb{D}$ and $F=\Phi_\varphi$ its Roper--Suffridge extension to $\mathbb{B}^n$, $n\ge2$. Then, for $z=(z_1,z')\in\mathbb{B}^n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normaRS}
\|S_F(z)\|=\frac{(1-|z_1|^2)^{3/2}\,|z'|\,|S\varphi(z_1)|}{2\sqrt{n+1}},
\end{equation}
and therefore
\[
\|S_F\|=\frac{\|S\varphi\|}{2\sqrt{n+1}},
\]
where $\|S\varphi\|$ is the classical norm \eqref{eq:normaclasica}. In particular, if $\varphi$ is convex then $\|S_F\|\le1/\sqrt{n+1}$, with equality when $\varphi(\mathbb{D})$ is a strip, and if $\varphi$ is univalent then $\|S_F\|\le3/\sqrt{n+1}$.
<!-- end thm-24 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:SRS}, $\|S_F(z)(v,v)\|_z=\tfrac12|S\varphi(z_1)|\,|v_1|^2\,\|(0,z')\|_z$. From \eqref{eq:bergmanbola},
\[
\|(0,z')\|_z^2=\frac{n+1}{(1-|z|^2)^2}\bigl[(1-|z|^2)|z'|^2+|z'|^4\bigr]=\frac{(n+1)(1-|z_1|^2)\,|z'|^2}{(1-|z|^2)^2}.
\]
It remains to maximize $|v_1|^2$ over the vectors of Bergman norm one. The matrix of the metric is $\frac{n+1}{(1-|z|^2)^2}\bigl[(1-|z|^2)I+\overline z\,z^t\bigr]$, its inverse is $\frac{1-|z|^2}{n+1}\bigl[I-\overline z\,z^t\bigr]$, and the required maximum is the first diagonal entry of the inverse, that is,
\[
\max_{\|v\|_z=1}|v_1|^2=\frac{(1-|z|^2)(1-|z_1|^2)}{n+1}.
\]
Multiplying, we obtain \eqref{eq:normaRS}. Since $|z'|^2<1-|z_1|^2$, with supremum $1-|z_1|^2$, it follows that
\[
\sup_{z'}\|S_F(z_1,z')\|=\frac{(1-|z_1|^2)^2\,|S\varphi(z_1)|}{2\sqrt{n+1}}.
\]
The rest follows from $\|S\varphi\|\le2$ for convex functions \cite{CDO} and from $\|S\varphi\|\le6$ for univalent functions.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- prob-1: body_md -->
The bound \eqref{eq:curvaturabergman} gives, for the mappings of $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$, a control of the Euclidean curvature of the preimages of hyperplanes. Can one obtain from it, by a geometric argument, a criterion for univalence, that is, that two of these preimages in general position meet in at most one point?
<!-- end prob-1 -->
<!-- prob-2: body_md -->
Determine the order and the norm order of $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ in $\mathbb{B}^n$. Between Theorems~\ref{thm:ordensup} and~\ref{thm:ordeninf} there is a gap in the dependence on $n$, and the characteristic equation \eqref{eq:carac1}--\eqref{eq:carac2} contains more information than has been used.
<!-- end prob-2 -->
<!-- prob-3: body_md -->
Determine the largest $\alpha_0(n)$ for which $\|S_F\|\le\alpha_0$ implies univalence in $\mathbb{B}^n$. Theorem~\ref{thm:univCH15} gives a value of order $n^{-3/2}$, determined by the condition $\delta(n,\alpha_0)<1$ of \eqref{eq:delta}. By Theorem~\ref{thm:RSbola}, the Roper--Suffridge extensions of nonunivalent functions with $\|S\varphi\|$ slightly larger than $2$ show that $\alpha_0(n)\le1/\sqrt{n+1}$. The correct order of magnitude is not known.
<!-- end prob-3 -->
<!-- prob-4: body_md -->
Construct in the polydisk a density associated with the solutions of \eqref{eq:sistema} that is invariant and convex with respect to the Bergman metric, or show that none exists. A complete Ahlfors--Weill extension in $\mathbb{D}^n$ depends on this. In the same vein, what is the optimal constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:poli}?
<!-- end prob-4 -->
<!-- prob-5: body_md -->
Determine $\sup\{\|S_F\|:\ F\in K(\mathbb{B}^n)\}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:RSbola} it is at least $1/\sqrt{n+1}$. Is the Roper--Suffridge extension of the strip extremal?
<!-- end prob-5 -->
<!-- prob-6: body_md -->
Find a closed expression for the constant $\gamma_n$ of \eqref{eq:Lambda} when $n\ge3$. It is the best possible bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:convexaspoli}.
<!-- end prob-6 -->
